overview: A weak system brings light snow Saturday into Sunday, then a break Monday. A stronger system arrives Tuesday, with Tuesday through Wednesday the main window for snow across the Cascades and the Sierra.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A weak disturbance brings light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the mountains from Saturday evening into Sunday, with little impact. The main event comes Tuesday as a frontal system moves in, snow levels rising to the valley floor during the day. Mt. Baker leads the region with 15 inches over the window, and Crystal Mountain sees its biggest day Tuesday.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: A weak Sunday system brings light snow with a rain mix in the valleys. A stronger system arrives Tuesday, with snow likely Tuesday through Wednesday, possibly heavier than the Sierra forecast. Sugar Bowl sees the most snow in the area at 13 inches. The NWS is calling for more, 11 to 21 inches Sunday through Wednesday night.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Periods of snow Saturday night taper to flurries Sunday and Monday. Rain moves in Tuesday night and holds through Wednesday, with snow levels high. Whistler sees the most, 15 inches over the window, mostly from snow on Tuesday.

regions.title: Eastern Sierra
regions.text: Sunday brings a fast-moving system with cold air keeping snow levels low and little moisture, so totals stay modest but travel is hard Sunday evening. Monday afternoon through Tuesday evening is the best travel window. Snow returns Tuesday night into Wednesday. Mammoth sees 9 inches, with its biggest day Sunday.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
